repulsive

rih-PUL-siv -- shares a root with 'propel,' meaning to push or drive. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Repulsive is arousing intense distaste or disgust.

Even seasoned health inspectors found the odor coming from the abandoned freezer utterly repulsive.

Example

A pile of spoiled food left in the sun for a week develops a smell so repulsive that everyone walking past instinctively covers their nose and hurries away.

That instinctive urge to recoil is what marks the smell as repulsive. Unlike 'unpleasant,' which can be mild, repulsive is strong enough to make people physically pull back.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

revolting: Revolting means causing strong disgust, and it is the closest everyday twin of repulsive. The shade of difference: repulsive emphasizes the push-away reaction -- people physically drawing back -- while revolting emphasizes how vile the thing itself is.

nauseating: Nauseating means turning the stomach -- making you feel physically sick, whether from a foul smell, a gruesome sight, or a lurching motion. Repulsive is about disgust and recoil: a repulsive thing makes people pull back, even when nobody actually feels ill.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

appealing: attractive or pleasing

delightful: causing great pleasure

Where it sits · how deep the disgust runs — off-putting → repulsive → loathsome

off-putting vs. repulsive: Off-putting is much milder than repulsive -- an off-putting habit just makes you want a little distance, while something repulsive makes people physically recoil in disgust.

loathsome vs. repulsive: Loathsome can feel even stronger than repulsive: repulsive focuses on the disgusted physical reaction something causes, while loathsome adds a deeper, more personal sense of hatred toward it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back (Latin)

Root — puls

Root — puls: to push, drive (from Latin pellere, past stem puls- -- the same root that appears as -pel- in propel)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: having the quality of (Latin -ivus)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin repellere meant 'to drive back': re- ('back') + puls (from pellere, 'to push, drive') + -ive ('having the quality of'). Something repulsive, at its root, pushes you back and away from it -- the same Latin root that appears as -pel- in propel.

Use the root in a new word: propel

Use the root in a new word: propel: It took two rocket boosters to propel the probe out of Earth's orbit.
